say.text: Step one: what does the tumour touch? A 3 cm lump has **peau d'orange** (orange-peel skin) over it, with no redness or warmth.
Which T category is it?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Peau d'orange is skin involvement, so it is T4b, and a skin sign outranks size.
Size bands run T1 up to 2 cm, T2 over 2 to 5 cm, T3 over 5 cm; skin or chest-wall spread moves the case to T4.
That choice is not right.
Peau d'orange is the sign people link with inflammatory cancer, but the sign alone is skin involvement, not the whole picture of T4d.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so fix the belief: a sign is not the syndrome. Look at the whole breast before you name T4d.

say.text: That choice is not right.
Size is the first thing people check, but a skin sign is decided before size, so the 3 cm alone does not settle it.
Ask two things: what does the lump touch, and what does the skin show? Then ask whether the whole breast is red, warm and swollen.
Step two: the chest wall. Which finding makes the tumour chest-wall disease, T4a?

choices.label: Tumour fixed to pectoralis major alone
Satellite skin nodules over the breast
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. T4a is chest-wall extension into ribs, intercostal muscles or serratus anterior, not the pectoralis major.
Fixity to the pectoralis is tested with the muscle contracted; fixity alone does not make T4a.
That choice is not right.
The pectoralis is the muscle the tumour touches first, so fixity feels like chest-wall spread, but it is not in the T4a set.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so fix the belief: a muscle the tumour touches is not the same as the chest wall it invades.

say.text: That choice is not right.
Satellite nodules are real T4 criteria, so they tempt, but skin findings belong to T4b, not to the chest wall.
Think about the structures under the breast, not the skin on top. Which of them could the tumour grow into?
Step three: the nodes. Ipsilateral nodes lie above the collarbone and nothing else is distant. Which category?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Ipsilateral supraclavicular nodes are N3c, regional disease, and M0 if nothing else is distant.
The ladder: N1 mobile axillary, N2a fixed axillary, N2b internal mammary, N3a infraclavicular, N3c supraclavicular.
That choice is not right.
Nodes above the collarbone feel far from the breast, and old exam keys counted them as distant disease, but they are still regional nodes.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so replace the old key: current staging keeps these nodes regional, and M1 needs disease beyond them.

say.text: That choice is not right.
Infraclavicular nodes are a real station, but they sit below the collarbone, and this node sits above it.
Find where the node sits against the collarbone, then match that position to a level on the ladder.
Step four: the work-up. A 38-year-old has a 1.5 cm core-proven invasive ductal carcinoma. The axilla is clinically node-negative and she has no symptoms. What next?

choices.label: Skip metastatic imaging; plan local treatment
Order a whole-body bone scan first
Start serum CA 15-3 as a staging test
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Routine metastatic imaging is not needed in early asymptomatic disease; it is for locally advanced disease or symptoms.
That choice is not right.
Bone is the commonest site of spread, which makes a bone scan feel thorough, but where cancer usually spreads is not a reason to scan every patient.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check your reason: a common site of spread does not trigger imaging; the stage and the symptoms do.

say.text: That choice is not right.
CA 15-3 is a tumour marker that follows metastatic disease once it is known; it does not screen or stage an early cancer.
Ask what the stage and the symptoms are before you think of any scan, then pick the step this case actually calls for.
Bone is the commonest site of distant spread, mostly **osteolytic**; lung, liver and brain follow.
The most important prognostic factor is **axillary lymph node status**.
